For a simple (usually unsigned) OCSP request : we have 2 hash values (issuerCertHash, serialNumberHash), and

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Analogous content about CRL and the CRL Distribution Points is at https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5280/#section-4.2.1.13

If only HTTP is used, the same things as in RFC 6960 and RFC 5280 can be said for messages that transfer C509-related information (e.g., about the request method that can be used).

At the same time, when querying an OCSP server, it should be the case that a caching-oriented, idempotent, and safe request is actually desired (in contrast with a POST request), while also not resorting to encoding the request content in the query component of the target URI of a GET request. So, if CoAP is used at all, the following can be considered:

* If both the server and the client use CoAP, requests can then use the FETCH request method (RFC 8132), with all its advantages compared to the stretched use of POST (or of GET with query parameters).

* If not both the server and client use CoAP (likely, the server is the one that uses HTTP) and a cross-proxy is deployed in between, we need the requests to be GET or POST (with the resulting downsides discussed in RFC 8132), since there is no defined translation between FETCH and a corresponding HTTP method (one day, the recent QUERY could be considered, see RFC 10008).

Regarding security and the current era, it's probably about strongly discouraging unsecure communication, whatever the transfer protocol used.

A few things to consider if cacheability of responses is desired:

* For OCSP requests, they should practically need to converge on nonce=null in order to set the ground for producing a cache hit.

* If OSCORE-based security is used, cacheability of responses is possible by using the variant of Group OSCORE defined in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-core-cacheable-oscore/

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body:
Thank you Lijun & Rikard! A few inputs from the constrained-IoT side, now that I'm (partially) back from summer vacation :)

About the motivation / "industry need" / "comparison with alternatives":
 
I think we can state the gap (more) concretely, to make it clear that for constrained devices over 6LoWPAN/LPWAN, the practical alternative today is often no revocation at all. DER X.509 CRL and HTTP-based OCSP are too large and too many round-trips for the link budget. Framing the contribution as ~"enables [standard based] revocation where it was previously impractical" is a stronger claim, but justified, in addition to "smaller and easier to process" alone.

About CRLite, and possibly as a broader conclusion for the alternative section: The section already notes CRLite as a compressed, browser-oriented filter, which functions as client-side, non-interoperable local structures. And this is why a standard, certificate-type-agnostic wire format for full per-certificate status structures is a missing piece, which doesn't compete with CRLite but rather complements it. 

Multi-vendor point, agreeing with your comment Lijun: Even single-operator constrained deployments are in need of mixing silicon and/or stacks, so reusing standard, open-source-friendly modules (one C509 parser, COSE signatures, OSCORE) should be the way forward also there. Maybe also worth a sentence in the motivation.

On OAuth/token status lists: agree they target a different problem (issuer-assigned index over a bounded population) and aren't a like-for-like alternative, so I wouldn't expand the section for them. 

Related / FYI: I'm looking into a first implementations, let's soon discuss what we want a reference implementation to demonstrate!

issues.author: lijun-nio

In the current draft, we register our own hash algorithms.

Another direction is to use the algorithm codes defined in COSE algorithms (which is a collection of all algorithm types, including hash, signature, encrytion, KDF, ...).

 @marco-tiloca-sics @rikard-sics @highlunder  @comsats

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
TL;DR: My impression is that the current structure of the registry "C509 Hash Algorithms" is as intended and aligned with other registries in the new C509 ecosystem.


Looking at the new registry "C509 Hash Algorithms" defined in the draft:

* In spite of its name, its entries don't indicate only hash algorithms, but rather a bundle of information about hash algorithms.

  At the same time, it's really aligned with the spirit of other C509 registries, e.g., "C509 Signature Algorithms" [1] that has the same fields with reference to signature algorithms.

* Like for the registry at [1], I thought that the intent was to be able to use also algorithms that are not registered in the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2].

  E.g., for "C509 Hash Algorithms", see the entry with 'Value' = 3 for "SHA-224"; for "C509 Signature Algorithms" [1], see the entry with 'Value' = 8 for "SM2 with SM3".

  If the idea is instead to limit the C509 Hash Algorithms specifically to hash algorithms that are also registered in the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2] (although I haven't had that impression so far), then their 'Value' in the "C509 Hash Algorithms" could indeed use the same value that the corresponding algorithm has in the 'Value' column of the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2] (e.g., -16 for "SHA-256"). However, thinking of fields like 'hashAlgorithm' defined in the draft, this also results in having less control when it comes to prioritizing values according to the most efficient, desired encoding in CBOR.


[1] https://www.iana.org/assignments/cbor-encoded-x509-c509#c509-signature-algorithms

[2] https://www.iana.org/assignments/cose#algorithms

issues.title: Resolving the Name / #6.121 encoding ambiguity in C509 CRLs
issues.author: lijun-nio
issues.body:
**In draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert:**

```
Name = [ * RDNAttribute ] / SpecialText

SpecialText = text / bytes / tag
```

**In this draft**, the CRL structure has the following definitions:

```
authoritySubject       : Name / #6.121(bytes),

issuer                 : Name / #6.121(bytes) / null,
```

This creates an ambiguity. `#6.121` (the tag for alternative 0) is meant to mark a DER-encoded X.509 name, but because `SpecialText` allows `tag`, the same encoding can also be parsed as a `Name`. I see two ways to solve this:

**Option 1: Update draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert.** Specify that a name consisting of a single commonName, which is currently encoded using the tag alternative, is instead encoded as `[ * RDNAttribute ]`.

- Pros:
  - Names in certificates and CRLs use the same encoding, so they can be matched byte for byte.
- Cons:
  - Requires a change to the C509 base specification.

**Option 2: Define a new CDDL type in this draft**, e.g. `RDNAttributes`:

```
RDNAttributes = [ * RDNAttribute ]

authoritySubject       : RDNAttributes / #6.121(bytes),

issuer                 : RDNAttributes / #6.121(bytes) / null,
```

- Pros:
  - No change to the C509 base specification is needed.
- Cons:
  - If a certificate's Name consists of a single commonName attribute, it must be re-encoded before it can be compared with the CRL's name.

Which option would the you prefer?
@marco-tiloca-sics @highlunder @comsats 

@rikard-sics : Maybe we could bring this up during the COSE WG presentation?

comments.author: rikard-sics
comments.body: Yes we could raise this during the IETF 127 presentation and see if the WG has any preferred solution

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
At this stage of the process, I easily prefer Option 2: it avoids changing draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert and it is "cleaner" as it defines what the data model needs here (acknowledging that a non-ambiguous reuse of `Name` is not possible). Sure, the mentioned re-enconding is not nice.

However, the change proposed as Option 1 is about forcing the use of `[ * RDNAttribute ]` for a name that consists of a single commonName.

Can't the same reasoning be incrementally applied to Option 2 and evolve it into the following Option 3?

```
RDNAttributes = [ * RDNAttribute ]

authoritySubject       : RDNAttributes,

issuer                 : RDNAttributes / null,
```

In other words, if it is in principle acceptable that C509 certificates could use the tag alternative instead of using `[ * RDNAttribute ]` also for a name consisting of a single commonName, can't the same be acceptable for the CRL structure here? Is this perhaps a backward compatibility issue for CRL responders?

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body: Option 3 does not provide the option to support X.509 Name.

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Thanks, got it (and, of course, X.509 Name is not in the scope of draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert).

Then `#6.121(bytes)` needs to stay around to ensure that the compact CRL structure works also when X.509 certificates are involved.

comments.author: xipki
comments.body:
What about the following CDDL definition?

```
NameChoice = [type int, name Defined]

-- For type 0: name = Name (C509 Name defined in the C509 base draft)
-- For type 1: name = bstr (DER-encoded X.509 name)

authoritySubject       : NameChoice,

issuer                 : NameChoice / null,
```

We need to add new IANA registry to register the type for NameChoice.
With this suggestion, it is still possible to compare octet-by-octet between CRL and C509 certificate / X509 certificate.

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Thanks, I think that that direction would work! See below a completed and revised version, also renaming NameChoice to NameVariant.


```
Name = [ * RDNAttribute ] / SpecialText
; from draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert

SpecialText = text / bytes / tag
; from draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert

NameVariant = [type: int, name: any]

authoritySubject       : NameVariant,

issuer                 : NameVariant / null,
```

As to type within NameVariant:
* 0: the `name` element has type `Name`
* 1: the `name` has type `bstr` (the DER-encoded X.509 name)

Yes, a new registry is needed for the values of the `type` element of the NameVariant array. I guess that the intent is only to map a value of `type`to a type of CBOR data item (e.g., `bstr`) and not necessarily with something as specific as a DER-encoded X.509 name.

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body:
Did you get any feedback from the IETF meeting?

In any case: 

`NameVariant = [type: int, name: any]` works for me: it is unambiguous, it keeps the X.509 case, and the C509 name inside it is still byte-for-byte the name from the certificate.

Two remarks:

1. Cost. It adds two bytes to every name (array header and type). That is small, but it applies to every CRL, so the size tables and all CRL examples change.

2. About registry. I would be fine with reusing "TLS Certificate Types" (X.509 = 0, C509 = 4) as proposed in #29 instead of creating a registry. The name would then be encoded as names are encoded in certificates of that type. If so, we probably want to explicitly state that only 0 and 4 are used in this document, since not every registered type has a name encoding. The numbering is then 0 = DER-encoded X.509 Name, 4 = C509 Name, the reverse of the proposal above. The CDDL could spell out both cases, which would let a tool check the `name` element:

   ```
   NameVariant = [ type: 0, name: bytes ] / [ type: 4, name: Name ]
   ```

I will update the Rust implementation when this is decided.

issues.title: Serial Number in the OCSP responses
issues.author: xipki
issues.body:
Currently we use `HashId20` (trunctat hash value) over the serial number. I discussed this with some PKI industry experts, and they wish us to use the raw serial number instead. The main reasons are
- OCSP database needs to have columns to contain HashId20 of the serial numbers. This is difficult to implement. The hash algorithms may vary from OCSP request to request (it is specified in the field `hashAlgorithm`), so the database needs to be extended to have multiple HashId20 columns (each column for one supported hash algorithm). And new algorithms may be registered in the future, and once the database schema is created, it is quite difficult to change it by adding new columns.
- Our proposal supports also X.509, that means the software needs to support old existing OCSP database, which do not contain such HashId20 columns.
- The current codebase for X.509 OCSP uses serial number, there are lots of work to support HashId20.
- The benefit of privacy of using hash value is limited. If one collects enough serial numbers, it can still find the serial number according to the hash value (via look-up).

I needs your input. @rikard-sics  @highlunder @marco-tiloca-sics @comsats.

@rikard-sics : should we also add this point to your presentation slides?

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Given the points above (especially the second and third), it seems unavoidable to use serial numbers for being compatible with how the back-end works.

For the sake of the argument:

* The second and third points show that any deviation from raw serial numbers is basically out of question. However ...

* For the case in the first point, it's not necessarily required to have one column per supported algorithm. There can still be a single column with an extensible semantics, e.g., encoding pairs (HashAlgorithmId, HashValue).

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body:
I support using the serial number itself.

From the constrained-client side it is an improvement, not a cost:

- The client does not have to hash the serial number.
- The message does not grow. `serialNumberHash` is always 20 bytes; a serial number is at most 20 bytes and usually shorter.
- The match becomes exact. The rule that a responder must not return `good` when a `serialNumberHash` matches more than one serial number is no longer needed.
- It is consistent with the C509 CRL, which already carries serial numbers in the clear.

I agree that the privacy argument is weak: the hash is unsalted, so anyone with a set of candidate serial numbers can identify the certificate. The Security Considerations already say that requests and responses should be protected (DTLS, OSCORE) or stapled where this matters, and that remains the answer.

Things to update if we do this:

- Encoding: the serial number as a byte string in big-endian order without a leading zero byte, as in C509 certificates, so that the value can be copied from the certificate.
- The overview bullet that lists hashed serial numbers as a privacy feature, and the paragraphs on `serialNumberHash` in the Security Considerations.
- OCSP examples.
- I assume `HashId20` itself can go.

I will adapt the Rust implementation (c509rev) once the CDDL is settled.

issues.title: Implementation feedback: X.509 example fixes and unspecified receiver behavior
issues.author: ligefeiBouncycastle
issues.body:
I implemented the CRL, CRLInfo and OCSP structures of the draft (at 8a34532) as a local prototype. All 14 examples parse and re-encode byte for byte, the 11 signatures verify and re-sign identically with the example keys, and every certificate hash matches. The points below came up along the way.

### Examples

1. The X.509 CRL examples have no extensions at all:
   - None of them has cRLNumber or authorityKeyIdentifier (both MUST, RFC 5280 Sections 5.2.3 and 5.2.1).
   - The delta CRL has no deltaCRLIndicator, so it is a full CRL that carries removeFromCRL entries.
   - The indirect CRL has no issuingDistributionPoint with indirectCRL TRUE (Section 5.2.5).
   - The C509 CRL with expiredCertsOnCRL has no X.509 counterpart of it.

   I rebuilt the four with these extensions and re-signed them with the example keys. They are 196, 496, 485 and 559 bytes, so the reductions are 38%, 47%, 49% and 47%, not 17%, 38%, 41% and 40%.
2. In every X.509 OCSP example except the error response, the nonce extnValue is the raw 16-byte nonce, not the DER of `Nonce ::= OCTET STRING` (RFC 6960 Section 4.4.1). The nonce is also shorter than the 32 octets RFC 9654 requires of requesters. Each X.509 message would grow by 2 bytes, or 18 with a 32-byte nonce.
3. The two signed request examples that carry the requestor's certificate (and chain) send AcceptableResponseTypes `[0, 1]`. By the text, that ranks the error response as the most preferred type, and type 0 "does not need to be listed". `[1]` would match the X.509 requests, which list only id-pkix-ocsp-basic.
4. The Introduction says C509 OCSP messages are "40% to 69% smaller", but the table includes 71% (Unsigned Basic OCSP Request).

### Text

1. dateLength: "the offset MUST fit within the specified byte length without leading zero bytes" cannot hold when the largest offset is 0. That happens with one entry dated at the RECOMMENDED baseDate, which needs dateLength 1 and the byte 0x00. The delta example's first entry is `0000`. Suggest: "dateLength is the smallest number of bytes that holds the largest offset in revokedCerts and removedFromCRLCerts (1 if all offsets are 0)". Say the same for serialNumberLength, across both lists.
2. With dateLength 0, the draft does not say what baseDate holds, although the field is mandatory and the notBefore rule still applies to it. The value then carries no information. Suggest: baseDate MUST be 0 and receivers ignore it, with the notBefore rule not applying (see the next item).
3. "baseDate MUST be greater than or equal to the issuer certificate's notBefore" has three problems:
   - It does not say which certificate applies in an indirect CRL.
   - A receiver cannot check it without that certificate.
   - After a CA certificate is renewed with a later notBefore, an earlier revocation date can no longer be encoded.

   Suggest dropping it, or replacing it with "baseDate MUST NOT be later than the earliest date in the entries".
4. removedFromCRLCerts is not excluded from a full CRL. RFC 5280 Section 5.3.1 allows removeFromCRL only in delta CRLs. Suggest: MUST be null when baseCrlNumber is null.
5. Nothing forbids two PerIssuerRevokedCerts for the same issuer, or a serial number that appears twice (within revokedCerts, or in both lists). A binary search then returns one of them arbitrarily. Suggest MUST NOT, and "strictly ascending" for bit 0.
6. The draft does not say what a receiver does with reason byte 7, 8 or above 10 in revokedCerts, or in RevokedInfo.revocationReason (uint8). Suggest: reject.
7. IntExtension keeps only the int branch of the C509 Extension and drops the ~oid branch, so a CRL or OCSP extension without a registry value cannot be carried at all. The draft does not say whether this is deliberate. If it is, please say so and say how an unregistered extension is to be handled. If not, add the ~oid branch, as in C509 certificates. This affects:
   - issuingDistributionPoint: it has neither a field nor a value. The issuer field of PerIssuerRevokedCerts stands in for indirectCRL, but distributionPoint, onlyContainsUserCerts, onlyContainsCACerts and onlySomeReasons have no equivalent. So scoped or partitioned CRLs cannot be expressed, and the scope checks of RFC 5280 Section 6.3.3 cannot be applied.
   - issuerAltName, freshestCRL and authorityInfoAccess: Table "CRL extensions" marks them "-", although the C509 Extensions registry has 25, 29 and 9. Please say whether those values may be used in crlExtensions.
   - invalidityDate: it has no per-entry place in a CRL, and it is common with keyCompromise. In OCSP, RFC 6960 Section 4.4.5 allows the CRL entry extensions as singleExtensions, but Table "OCSP extensions" leaves out Section 4.4.5, and the single response extensions have no value for invalidityDate either.

   There is also no rule that an extensionID appears only once.
8. Two cases where NameVariant for the issuer is not defined:
   - A C509 certificate whose issuer field is null (self-issued, e.g. a key rollover certificate) has no "issuer field" to copy. Suggest "the issuer name (the subject when issuer is null)".
   - For a type 3 certificate, the CRL section does not say whether to use NameVariant type 0 or 4, although the OCSP section treats type 3 as X.509.
9. signatureAlgorithm should exclude id-alg-unsigned (5) and the ECDH PoP algorithms (14 to 16): neither gives a signature a relying party can check. In C509BasicOCSPRequest, 5 would be a second way to say "unsigned" next to null.
10. hashAlgorithm is typed IntAlgorithmIdentifier, which the draft defines as the int form of the C509 AlgorithmIdentifier, but its values come from the COSE Algorithms registry. A separate alias, e.g. `COSEHashAlgorithm = int16`, would avoid reading it against the wrong registry.
11. "An OCSP responder MUST use in a response the same issuerCertHash value as in the corresponding request" only works if the response uses the request's hashAlgorithm, but that is not stated. Also, nothing says what a receiver does when the first certificate in requestorCerts or responderCerts does not match requestorCertHash or responderCertHash. Suggest: reject.
12. TN Query is "allowed only in the single-request extensions", so C509SimpleOCSPRequest, the only request type clients MUST support, cannot carry it. A STIR client must then use C509BasicOCSPRequest, which clients only MAY support. Either allow TN Query in the Simple request's extensions, or say STIR clients MUST support Basic.
13. responseStatus: the CDDL allows -128..127, but the table gives successful no value and defines only 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6. Say how a receiver treats any other value, such as `[0, 0]`, an error response whose status reads as successful. Suggest: reject.
14. Serial number normalization is only a sender rule. Say a responder returns malformedRequest for a serialNumber with a leading zero byte, as it does for serial number 0.
15. PEM labels: the "Textual Encoding Label" registry under "PKIX Parameters" does not exist (as already noted for additions).

pulls.title: Initial reference implementation for CBOR Encoded Certificate Revocation Management
pulls.author: highlunder
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR contributes **`c509rev`**, an open-source Rust reference implementation of the **C509 CRL** and **C509 OCSP** structures defined in this document: encode, decode, sign, verify, and the PEM textual representation. Correctness is checked by byte-exact known-answer tests against the draft's worked examples. The crate is self-contained and lives as the `c509rev/` subdirectory. This setup is mirroring the format `c509_demo_impl/` used for `cose-wg/CBOR-certificates`.

## Coverage

- **C509 CRL** — `CRLInfo` plus per-issuer revoked/removed entries with fixed-width, binary-searchable entry packing; delta and indirect CRLs; forward-delta `nextUpdate`.
- **C509 OCSP request** — Simple, Unsigned, and Signed.
- **C509 OCSP response** — Error, Basic, and Simple.
- **Signing / verification** — Ed25519 and ECDSA with NIST P-256, over the CBOR TBS.
- **PEM textual representation** — RFC 7468 `-----BEGIN C509 CRL / OCSP REQUEST / OCSP RESPONSE-----` for all three object types (RFC 4648 base64, no extra dependency).
- **Experimental** — a C509 Status List primitive, as a compact complement to the CRL.

## Validation

- Every draft worked example **decodes and re-encodes byte-for-byte**, including the original signature bytes (deterministic-CBOR round-trip).
- For signed objects, the encode KAT is a **TBS byte-match**, because the draft ships no example signing keys. In addition, the published `crlocsp-ca` Ed25519 key reproduces the exact `signatureValue` of the no-revoked CRL example — a full cross-implementation check — and is verified against the published CA public key.
- Ed25519 and ECDSA-P256 sign↔verify round-trips, with tamper and TBS-change rejected.

## Dependencies, layout, and licensing

- **Self-contained.** Depends only on `serde_cbor`, `sha2`, `hex`, `ed25519-dalek`, and `p256`, with **no dependency on the C509 certificate crate**. The few primitives it reuses — a deterministic CBOR encoder, the two v1-profile signature-algorithm ids, and Ed25519/ECDSA-P256 TBS signing — are carried locally (`src/lcbor.rs`, vendored verbatim under BSD-3-Clause with attribution; `src/registry.rs`; `src/sign.rs`), so it builds in a fresh clone with no sibling checkout.
- **Layout.** The crate lives as the `c509rev/` subdirectory, mirroring `c509_demo_impl/` in `cose-wg/CBOR-certificates`.
- **Licensing.** BSD-3-Clause.

## Robustness and security

- The decoder is hardened against malformed input: `revokedCertsControl.serialNumberLength` (`1..=20`) and `dateLength` (`0..=8`) are range-checked per the draft CDDL **before** they size entry strides and per-entry sub-slices (an oversized value could otherwise panic — a DoS), and `baseDate + offset` uses checked arithmetic.
- A **"Security considerations & known limitations"** section in the README records what was reviewed sound (no `unsafe`; CBOR parsing returns errors rather than panicking; sound signature verification) and the remaining items: residual CDDL value-range checks are a tracked conformance TODO; `serde_cbor` is unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2021-0127); and the 8-byte identity-hash truncation is a draft-level size/security trade-off.

## Testing

- `cargo test` — **45 passed, 0 failed, 0 warnings** (known-answer tests, decoder-hardening regression tests, and PEM tests including the RFC 4648 base64 vectors and PEM round-trips over the draft's worked CRL/OCSP examples).
- `cargo build --all-targets` — clean, 0 warnings.
- `cargo audit` — 0 vulnerabilities; the only advisory is the documented `serde_cbor` unmaintained notice.
- CLI (`bin/c509rev`) — `decode` / `verify` / `pem`, with hex- or PEM-encoded input auto-detected.

## Status

Reference and test tooling — not for production use. The implementation tracks the current draft revision and is intended to stay in sync as the specification evolves.

pulls.title: draft: one modification and one addition to Security Considerations
pulls.author: highlunder
pulls.body:
Two potential small additions to the Security Considerations section, each independent of the other, so either can be dropped.

1. **Signature Verification: deterministic encoding.** Verifying the signature over the bytes as received becomes a MUST (was SHOULD), and a message that is not deterministically encoded (the Terminology section already defines "CBOR" as deterministically encoded CBOR) MUST be rejected. Otherwise implementations can interpret the same signed bytes differently, and values computed over the encoding, such as cache keys, are not stable.

2. **New subsection Certificate Status.** `not-issued` and `unknown` do not assert that a certificate is valid, and a relying party MUST NOT treat them as `good`. A responder that knows that a serial number was not issued SHOULD return `not-issued` rather than `good`. This is a SHOULD because RFC 6960, Section 2.2, allows `good` for a serial number that was never issued.

reviews.body:
Thanks for pulling all of this together! I checked the CDDL, the field descriptions, the Security Considerations and the IANA section. Most of it matches what we discussed (plain serial number, `NameVariant` with the TLS certificate types, the merged request, the rename), and the merged request is clear about what the signature covers. Four points, the first two before this is merged:

**1. Implementation Status, implementation #1 (c509rev).** The entry now says "Version compatibility: draft-liao-cose-c509-revocation-02" and still says that the encoder output matches the examples byte for byte. The Rust code implements the structures on `main` (`serialNumberHash`, `HashId8`, separate unsigned and signed requests, `Name / #6.121`), so that is not true for the examples in this PR. I will update the implementation once the structures are settled. Until then, could the entry say -01, or could we hold the -02 submission until the implementation follows?

**2. Which bytes of the hash are kept.** On `main` a truncated identifier is "the leading" bytes of the hash; in this PR `HashId20` is the low-order 20 bytes, following IEEE 1609.2. I have no objection to that convention if we think it's relevant to follow, but the change is not in the PR description or in the list of changes from -01 to -02, and it changes every hash value in the examples and in existing implementations. Could it get its own line in the change list?

**3. `HashId8` to `HashId20`: the cost, for illustration.** From the examples in the two versions:

| Example | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| Simple OCSP request | 51 | 59 |
| Simple OCSP response | 140 | 160 |
| Unsigned basic request | 132 | 141 |
| Basic response without responder certificate | 248 | 268 |

The plain serial number saves 4 bytes in these examples and each 20-byte hash adds 12. With the serial number change alone, the simple request would be about 47 bytes and the simple response about 136; with 20-byte hashes they are 59 and 160. These two are the messages every client has to support.

On the security side, the new text in the Security Considerations says that the identifier "only selects a certificate and does not authenticate it; security relies on the signature verification", and that it has to be unique only among the CA and responder certificates a party knows. With 8 bytes the probability that any two of n certificates collide is about n^2 / 2^65: about 3 * 10^-14 for 1,000 certificates and 3 * 10^-8 for a million. 

Was this increased hash length requested at the IETF meeting? Otherwise I'm inclined to try to defend the shorter hashes.

**4. Raw public keys (#33).** This is new and has not been discussed. Was this brought up at IETF? Maybe it could deserve separate PR. One initial question:

- In a CRL the authority for raw public keys is a byte string "assigned by the deployment". In OCSP the issuer of a raw public key is identified by `issuerCertHash` over a `SubjectPublicKeyInfo`. How do the two relate, and who is "the issuer" of a raw public key?
